newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Limited effect seen from China crude tariff change.
newsitem.headline: Limited effect seen from China crude tariff change.

text.p: A change in the system of import tariffs for crude oil in China is expected to have a limited affect on demand, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Chinese oil companies are unlikely to need to adjust crude oil imports because of the change, company officials said on Tuesday.

China's State Council Customs Office said Beijing would implement a special import tariff on crude oil of 16 yuan ($1.90) per tonne from July 1, replacing a current tariff that imposes a 1.5 percent tariff on the value of the import.
The new system is aimed at complying with international practice, a customs official said.
The customs office said the tariff change was a proposal. A final decision would be made depending on industry comments.
"If we took the year of 1996 as a basis, the new tariff is actually lower than 1.5 percent on the import value," said an official with China Internatioal United Petroleum and Chemicals Corporation.
"We don't know what oil prices will be for the whole year this year, but even if we have to pay a higher tariff after July, it won't make much difference to us," the official added.
The China Daily said in January that China's crude oil imports in 1997 were seen rising to 34 million tonnes.
But analysts said imports could rise to 28 million tonnes, but doubted they would be much more than 30 million.
In 1996, imports were 22 million tonnes, customs data shows.
State figures show overal Chinese crude demand rising at 4.8 to 6.0 percent per year, which over time will put an increasing burden on imports, analysts said.
Sources at state importer China National Chemicals Import and Export Co (Sinochem) said they saw little impact from the new tariff.
"There may be some differences between the new and old tariff, but in any case, it should not be big," said one of the officials.

The official, who expected the cost for crude oil imports to go down slightly after the new system goes into effect, said there was no need for his company to increase or decrease crude imports in view of the tariff change.
Some sources said China might apply the new system to oil products in the future.
"Since now we follow the international trend on crude oil (about tariffs), I think it's quite possible that the new system will apply to products as well," an the official with Sinopec said.
China currently imposes a tariff on oil product imports based on a percentage of the value of the import.
